name: Ahwar of Southern Iraq (Mesopotamian Marshes)
blurb: Reed beds, buffalo and otters of the Tigris-Euphrates marshes.

tip.title: Cut the floodwater
tip.text: Drainage and dams starved the marshes of river flow. Set Tigris-Euphrates floodwater to -100% and watch the reeds, then the fish, birds and otters that depend on them.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage: The Ahwar of Southern Iraq

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Common reed
nodes.desc: The dominant marsh plant. Dense reed beds give nesting cover to birds such as the Basra reed warbler and supply the reeds the Marsh Arabs build with.

nodes.name: Southern cattail
nodes.desc: A tall emergent marsh plant that grows with reeds in the shallow water of the marshes.

nodes.name: Shining pondweed
nodes.desc: A submerged aquatic plant recorded in the marsh area, providing food and cover in open water.

nodes.name: Water buffalo
nodes.desc: Herded by marsh communities, buffalo graze and wade through the reed beds and wet meadows.

nodes.name: Marbled duck
nodes.desc: A threatened dabbling duck of shallow wetlands. The marshes are reported to hold a large share of the world population.

nodes.name: Common moorhen
nodes.desc: A secretive omnivorous waterbird of reed edges that eats plants and small animals.

nodes.name: Euphrates softshell turtle
nodes.desc: An opportunistic omnivore of rivers and marshes, eating crabs, plants, insects and fish and readily taking carcasses.

nodes.name: Mesopotamian barbel
nodes.desc: A large barbel of the Tigris-Euphrates system and a staple of marsh fisheries.

nodes.name: Non-biting midges
nodes.desc: Midge larvae live in marsh mud and water and are food for fish, dragonflies and reed-bed birds.

nodes.name: Basra reed warbler
nodes.desc: Breeds in dense reed and papyrus beds of the Tigris-Euphrates system. Drainage nearly destroyed its habitat and it is endangered.

nodes.name: Scarlet skimmer
nodes.desc: A dragonfly recorded in the marshes, hunting smaller flying insects over open water.

nodes.name: Pied kingfisher
nodes.desc: A fish-eating bird that hovers over open water and dives for small fish.

nodes.name: Great cormorant
nodes.desc: A diving fish-eater that is a common sight on marsh channels and open water.

nodes.name: Purple heron
nodes.desc: A reed-bed wader that stalks fish and frogs in shallow water.

nodes.name: Golden jackal
nodes.desc: An opportunistic hunter and scavenger of the marsh edges, taking birds, small animals and carrion.

nodes.name: Smooth-coated otter
nodes.desc: The Iraqi marsh population (subspecies maxwelli) eats mainly fish and was feared lost before tracks were found in 2009.

nodes.name: Western marsh harrier
nodes.desc: A raptor that hunts low over reed beds for waterbirds and other small prey.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Strong sun in a hot climate drives rapid plant growth in the shallow water.

nodes.name: Tigris-Euphrates floodwater
nodes.desc: The marshes depend on river flow. Drainage and upstream dams cut it, and reflooding after 2003 let wetlands partly recover.

nodes.name: River silt and nutrients
nodes.desc: Floodwater delivers silt and nutrients that feed reed beds.

nodes.name: Bacteria and fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead reeds, plants and animals, returning nutrients to the mud and water.

link_ideas.what: The marshes are a migratory stopover for waterbirds moving between Siberia and Africa.
